title.value: Efficient Proofs of Possession for Legacy Signatures
Efficient Proofs of Possession for Legacy Signatures

abstract.value: Digital signatures underpin identity, authenticity, and trust in modern computer systems. Cryptography research has shown that it is possible to prove possession of a valid message and signature for some public key, without revealing the message or signature. These proofs of possession work only for specially-designed signature schemes. Though these proofs of possession have many useful applications to improving security, privacy, and anonymity, they are not currently usable for widely deployed, legacy signature schemes-like RSA, ECDSA, and Ed25519. Unlocking practical proofs of possession for these legacy signature schemes requires closing a huge efficiency gap. This work brings proofs of possession for legacy signature schemes very close to practicality. Our design strategy is to encode the signature's verification algorithm as a rank-one constraint system (R1CS), then use a zkSNARK to prove knowledge of a solution. To do this efficiently we (1) design and analyze a new zkSNARK called Dorian that supports randomized computations, (2) introduce several new techniques for encoding hashes, elliptic curve operations, and modular arithmetic, (3) give a new approach that allows performing the most expensive parts of ECDSA and Ed25519 verifications outside R1CS, and (4) generate a novel elliptic curve that allows expressing Ed25519 curve operations very efficiently. Our techniques reduce R1CS sizes by up to 200× and prover times by more than 20×. We can generate a 240-byte proof of possession of an RSA signature over a message the size of a typical TLS certificate-two kilobytes-in only three seconds. 3291 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

We can generate a 240-byte proof of possession of an RSA signature over a message the size of a typical TLS certificate-two kilobytes-in only three seconds. 1. Introduction Digital signatures are the foundation of identity, authen- ticity, and trust in modern computer systems-on the web, several signatures are verified for every TLS connection, and signatures allow authenticating domain name records through DNSSEC. Signatures underpin user identity as well, through systems like OAuth and passkeys. Signatures secure software supply chains through code signing and are used to bootstrap trust in trusted execution environments. An extraordinarily useful design pattern for all these applications of signatures is proofs of possession (PoPs): being able to prove that you know a signature on some message without having to reveal it. The security, privacy, and anonymity benefits of proofs of signature possession are huge: they can make credentials more private [ 31, 51], allow untraceable anonymous payments [16], help people browse the internet anonymously [ 53], make X.509 certificates more secure [ 43], build better blocklisting [ 93, 103], combat misinformation [54, 78], and more [26, 38, 44, 68]. Cryptographers have spent decades building signature schemes with purpose-built efficient PoPs. A few of these schemes have seen limited real-world deployment (Idemix, BBS+ and CL signatures) [ 29, 33, 75] but for the signature schemes in widespread use-RSA-PKCS1v1.5, ECDSA- P256, and Ed25519 [ 62, 64, 66], with the SHA-256 and SHA-512 [61] hash functions-the state of the art is very poor; few advances have been made over naive baselines. Proofs of possession for these legacy signature schemes necessarily are all built using the template of [ 79]-roughly, they are non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proofs of knowledge for the statement “For public key pk, I know a verifying signature σ for message m”. Because legacy signature schemes involve several different kinds of computations-bit manipulations, arithmetic modulo small powers of two, arithmetic modulo large primes, arithmetic modulo composites, elliptic curve group operations-these NIZKs are necessarily built by representing verification in a generic encoding, such as rank-one constraint systems (R1CS), and then applying a NIZK for R1CS relations. However, R1CS encodings of the operations used in legacy signatures have huge overhead, leading to unusably slow proving and verifying. For example, in the seminal Cinderella work, proving possession of a single TLS certificate signed with RSA took 137 seconds [43]. Our results. We give the fastest known protocols for proving statements about legacy signature schemes. Relative to the prior state of the art, we improve: • RSA-PKCS1v1.5 proving time by ≥3× (with similar proof size), • ECDSA-P256-SHA256 proving time by ≥20× (with ≈10× smaller proofs), and • Ed25519 proving time by ≥4× (with ≈30kB proofs). For the same problem size as the Cinderella proof of possession described before, we are about 75 × faster than their reported prover time, though our numbers are on newer hardware. (The Cinderella authors did not respond to our repeated requests to release the code, so we are unable to reproduce their numbers on our hardware.) Our techniques lead to reductions of up to 200 × in constraint costs over baselines. We focus on the following concrete setting: given a public key pk as public input, the prover shows they know a hidden message/signature pair (m, σ) such that Vf(pk, m, σ) = 1. We conservatively assume that both the 3291 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00080 message and signature must be completely hidden. However, the flexibility of modern ZKPs makes our techniques easily extensible to other settings, such as one in which the public key is hidden (committed) and the message and (partial) signature are public. This setting arises when building ring signatures [ 36, 51, 58]. Indeed, we show our techniques lead to a ≈300× improvement over the state of the art for ECDSA-based ring signatures. Our main novel contributions are as follows: • a new zk-SNARK, Dorian; Dorian is an extension of Spartan [96] that supports verifier randomness • a new approach for optimizing the use of lookup tables in modular arithmetic, including formalizing “subrange sizing schemes” and designing the first optimizing table planner • a family of “sidecar” protocols for eliminating the main algebraic bottleneck from elliptic-curve-based signature verification, by securely moving expensive elliptic curve operations into an auxiliary protocol. We next describe these and other contributions in more detail. We structure this discussion with the observation that most signature schemes are hash-then-verify: they apply a cryptographic hash like SHA-256 to the message and then some “inner” verification procedure to the result. The inner procedure comprises group operations and modular arithmetic. (For example, in RSA-PKCS1v1.5, the inner procedure is modular exponentiation with the signer's pub- lic exponent, and the outer procedure is SHA-256 with PKCS1v1.5 padding.) We significantly optimize both hashing and verification via a combination of novel technical ideas and applications of, and extensions to, existing ones. Optimizing the inner verification. One of our key technical contributions is in optimizing ZKPs for elliptic- curve-based signatures, specifically ECDSA and Ed25519. The main efficiency bottleneck in building ZKPs for these schemes is the huge cost of checking curve operations, particularly scalar multiplications, with a ZKP. Naively, a single multiplication can add tens of seconds to proving time [59]. Verifying an ECDSA signature (see Figure 3) requires two scalar multiplications with different bases-one base is fixed and public, and the other is not fixed. Prior work has shown that scalar multiplications with fixed public bases can be sped up by preprocessing a table of multiples of the base [25], and that incomplete formulas can be used safely. We apply these ideas in Section 7. This yields important savings, but does not reduce costs enough for our purposes. Two bottlenecks remain: first, the dynamic-base scalar multiplication, which cannot be optimized via preprocessing; second, the overhead of expressing modular arithmetic operations in constraints over a “foreign” field. To understand this, note that ZKPs allow one to prove arithmetic constraints (sums and products) over a field Fp, for prime p. In general, each ZKP is designed and implemented to prove statements for specific choices of prime p; usually, the modular arithmetic performed in signatures is for a different choice of prime q. One way to avoid the overhead of emulating mod- q operations with mod- p constraints is to simply change the ZKP's field to Fq. (This idea is folklore; not novel.) Indeed, this “right-field” approach is a tool we use. However, applying this tool to legacy schemes requires some care. For efficiency reasons, many state-of-the-art ZKPs, including the popular Groth16 and Halo2 protocols, require the finite field Fp to have special structure-a point with multiplicative order a large power of two which can be used for FFTs. So, if the signature scheme's q does not have this structure, these popular protocols cannot be used over the “right-field” (S8.1). In settings where very small proofs are not necessary, this is not an issue, as other ZKPs (such as our new NIZK, Dorian) work over any group where discrete log is hard. For the latter setting, we use right-field arithmetic for ECDSA. To do this, we instantiate the Spartan ZKP [ 96] with a customized elliptic curve whose scalar field is Fq, for the q from P256. (This curve was found by prior work [ 51], where it was used for a different purpose.) This reduces the constraint cost of the algebraic part of the ECDSA signature verification by roughly 200 ×. For the former setting, we optimize the emulation of mod- q arithmetic. The bottleneck in existing arithmetic emulation designs is range-checking-verifying that a limb or carry x has not overflowed. Traditionally, range-checking is done bit- by-bit, which is expensive [ 71]. To optimize, we borrow the idea of range-checking through lookup tables [23]: building a table (set) T of all valid limb values, and checking x ∈ T . Applying this idea to arithmetic emulation is non-trivial, because arithmetic emulation requires different range checks of different sizes, and because lookups have large size- specific one-time overheads. To improve performance, we adjust the emulation to decompose ranges into sub-ranges of uniform size. We implement an optimizer that computes optimal subrange sizes ahead of time, to minimizes the proving-time overheads of the lookups ( S6.2). Lookup arguments give big improvement, but some group operations are still expensive. So, we design new protocols which move some group operations out of the general- purpose ZKP and into a “sidecar” sigma protocol. This idea is from Sigmabus [ 65], but with very different techniques. It requires a new sigma protocol for proving knowledge of a group element representation where one of the bases is hidden (but committed). Optimizing hashing. We use lookups again to optimize the hash functions used by all schemes. Our main contribution is designing a new way of using lookup tables for this setting: instead of choosing a static representation for intermediate values, we store them in one of three different representations and operate on representations efficiently using lookups. This has some overhead but it allows for different operation types (bitwise & arithmetic) to both be performed very efficiently. Other contributions. Along the way, we make a number of additional contributions. First, we extend the Spartan [ 96] proof system to build a novel generalization we call Dorian, which allows for proofs about computations with verifier- supplied randomness.
